forms:
March 7 — Sunny

Today I played with Kenta in the park.

Kenta says he’s gonna move soon, but he’ll come
back when he’s older.

We promised to play in the park again together
when we grow up.

I doubt anyone will ever read this, but the memories
of my experiences are too much to bear alone, so I’ve
decided to confide in this diary.

I’m a nameless hacker. I infiltrate the networks of
huge corporations, steal their secrets, and sell them
to their rivals.

I already have more than enough money,

but it’s fun peering behind the scenes, so it’s almost
like a hobby for me.

I donate all the money I don’t use to things like
Pokémon conservation groups.

Ever since I was a kid, I’ve liked computers and
Pokémon more than people.

My field survey on Cinnabar proved quite fruitful.

I spoke with Pokémon Professors from other regions
and gained a number of insights for my own research.

Many folks were very concerned about possible
effects the recent weather disturbances may be
having on Pokémon.

On my way home, I found a young Tangela.

He appeared injured and weak, so I used a Potion
to heal him. He seemed to take a liking to me and
toddled along behind me.

I wasn’t sure what to do at first. I ended up bringing
him home with me, figuring he might be a good
playmate for my grandchild.

The sea is really rough today. The ship keeps swaying
back and forth. And swaying...and swaying...

It’s all I can do to write in this diary right now, but...
Ugh... I don’t feel so good... I might not be able to
write much mo—

It happened when I was hacking into a server in
another region for fun and stumbled on a system
with excessively high security.

Finding these sorts of things is always a thrill.
It took a lot of effort, but once I breached it,
all I could find was what seemed like trivial data
about weather patterns.

It was anticlimactic, but it made me think...

Why would someone put so much effort into hiding
something like this? That nagged at me.

So I dove back in. It took a lot of work, but I learned
how to make sense of the weather data. I was able to
gather that a natural disaster had struck that region—
dozens of huge, repeated hurricanes.

That’s the only conclusion I could draw, but I’d never
heard news about a disaster like that.

My grandchild plays with Tangela a lot these days.
They both seem to be having so much fun. Just
watching them warms my heart.

Tangela shows interest in any and all human activities.
When I’m working on the computer, he stares intently
at my screen with a curious expression.

Trainers who come to visit me also play with
Tangela, and...

Tangela seems intrigued by the items they use. He
looks enthralled by things like Pokédexes and
Poké Balls.

Are all Tangela brimming with curiosity?
Or is this little one just special?

Pokémon really are fascinating. There’s always more
to learn about them!

May 7
I can’t think of anything! I need to have FOUR design
proposals ready in two days, but I’m coming up blank!

I was begging my Smeargle for help, and he scribbled
some random patterns on a piece of paper and
handed it to me. Are those design pitches? That’s
so cute!

Actually...that gives me an idea. Back to work!

If a disaster of that scale had really happened,
surely it would have received both local and
global attention.

With that thought, I remembered a foundation active
in that region.

They were known for their passion for Pokémon
conservation efforts. I had even donated to them.
I thought that an organization of that scale

might be able to influence media so that no news of
the disaster leaked outside the region.

I spent countless days infiltrating the foundation’s
servers, looking into any data I could lay my hands
on. And sure enough, it gradually became clear that
they were involved.

I finally fell asleep after repeated all-nighters.
When I woke up, I was surrounded by members of
the foundation.

Apparently I’d left traces when I hacked the servers.
That was enough for them to track me down.

The people from the foundation were surprisingly
polite, and they explained what was happening
in detail.

I have no intention of writing it all here.

The important thing is that someday this disaster
will spread throughout the entire world.

They said that humanity in its current state can’t
prevent it.

The foundation, together with other regions, had
formed a plan to evacuate all of humanity into space.
The plan was already in motion. My head was
spinning at the outrageous tale.

So what would become of Pokémon? When I put the
question to them, they described their “Pokémon
Conservation Project” and asked for my help.

While humanity is evacuated into space, all of the
Pokémon in the world are to be stored and protected
in a massive computer system. That is the Pokémon
Conservation Project.

An incredible plan. But the foundation members said
that in order to avoid panic they had to keep both
the disaster and the project out of the public eye as
much as possible.

Naturally this left them shorthanded.

Skilled computer technicians were in particularly
high demand.

That’s why the foundation sought me out after I
discovered the disaster—recruitment.

I took them up on their offer.

Until this point, I had always lived as I pleased.
But if I could save Pokémon using my skills, I had
to do it.

The work was tough but also rewarding.

Eventually, the public began to take notice of the
disaster. The foundation gradually evacuated
those who noticed to a “safe place,” but to avoid
panic, they waited until the last minute to tell people
that their destination was space.

In the middle of this unbelievable situation, I found
a flaw in the plan.

In order to escape the disaster, humanity would
temporarily take refuge in space while Pokémon
would be safely stored in a computer system.
This was the general overview of the plan.

But no computer system will keep running forever.

The foundation planned to send a select few
members back to the planet at regular intervals to

perform ongoing maintenance.

But for humanity to survive in space for any length of
time, it would take a tremendous amount of energy.
I calculated that even a slight deviation from the
original plan would result in insufficient energy to
return, leaving humankind stranded in space for
dozens, or even hundreds, of years.

If that happened, the essential system protecting the
Pokémon would eventually cease to function.

So I decided to add a little touch of my own to the
system’s programming.

First, it will continuously check the weather data
across the globe in search of environments that can
prove even slightly habitable to Pokémon.

Next, if maintenance is not performed for a long
period of time and the system begins to approach
its limits, it will release the Pokémon most suited
to those environments.

Of course, ideally humans will return someday and
live alongside Pokémon once more.

But on the off chance humanity never returns from
space...I think releasing the Pokémon into a wild
world rather than leaving them asleep in a computer
would be a happier outcome.

It may sound strange coming from the program’s
creator, but I hope it never has to run.

Today there was a gathering attended by Pokémon
Professors from every region. We had a surprising
announcement in store.

Increasingly intense weather abnormalities—and the
calamities striking each region as a result—show no
sign of slowing down.

At this rate, predictions suggest that we will no
longer be able to obtain enough food and energy
to continue living on this planet.

And we learned that a plan was secretly in motion to
evacuate all of humanity into space.

It also seemed that, with a few exceptions, it will not
be possible to bring Pokémon with us.

Of course some immediately raised their voices in
protest, which is when we heard about the Pokémon
Conservation Project.

It was decided that we will take part in the Pokémon
Conservation Project.

It’s a plan to safely store all Pokémon on the planet
in a massive computer system while humanity takes
refuge in space.

I can’t be sure that such a thing is even possible,
and being parted from our Pokémon will be terribly
painful, but...

this may be the only way that people and Pokémon
will be able to live together again someday.

I was also asked to join a survey team after we move
to space, but I held off on responding.

After humanity relocates, a small group will be sent
back to the planet to survey the environment and do
maintenance on the conservation system. But given
my age, I don’t know if I’ll still be spry enough to be
of much help. I think it’s a task best left to the young.

Something shocking has happened.

The Pokémon Conservation Project is progressing
smoothly, and the time came for my Tangela to join
the others.

In the hopes of avoiding a tearful scene, I waited until
my grandchild was asleep before entrusting Tangela
to one of the other project members. But later that
night, I received word that Tangela had run off.

Tangela was like family. He should have been
accustomed to humans. How could this have
happened?

I have a theory.
Tangela was likely trying to get back to our home.

But it’s nearly time for my family to set off for space.
Even if Tangela were to make it safely home...

by the time he arrives, we’ll no longer be there.

I feel agonizingly helpless knowing there’s nothing I
can do.

Nothing, that is, but hope that the project staff find
Tangela and keep him safe...

The day of departure finally arrived, and Tangela was
still nowhere to be found.

So I decided to join the survey team after all.

It will give me the opportunity to return to the planet
periodically, and I can search when I’m there.

If there are any strange machines or rare tools on the
ship, I should borrow them.

Then I’ll find Tangela and show them to him.

I’m certain he’ll examine them with his usual curiosity.

Until then...please, be safe.

March 13

Charlotte appears to be interested in cooking! I tried
teaching her a bit, and she’s really quite good at it.
She’s very dexterous with those little Greedent
hands, and it took almost no time before she was
able to help me out with simple tasks.

June 27

Charlotte’s an eager eater, but the one food she
doesn’t like is Chesto Berries. She made a rather
strained expression when I fed her some.

A chef shouldn’t be picky about things like that, but
I’d feel bad forcing her to eat something she doesn’t
like. What to do...

July 3

I made a special soup just for Charlotte using Chesto
Berries as a secret ingredient. She seemed to really
like it, and she appeared very satisfied as she finished
off the whole pot! I wonder how shocked she’d be if
she knew it had Chesto Berries. I look forward to the
day when she figures it out.
